terms.comment: In classical Latin two words, bene dīcere, to speak well of; as one word, “to bless”, it is the Church’s, from Tertullian and the Vulgate on (Lewis & Short). People and things are blessed in the accusative (benedīcēbat eōs); God is blessed, that is praised, in the accusative or, more rarely, the dative (Benedīc, anima mea, Dominō, Ps. 102 (103), 2).

phrases.latin: Benedīcat tibi Dominus, et custōdiat tē.
phrases.english: The Lord bless you and keep you (the blessing at bedtime, a hand on the child’s head).

phrases.latin: Et complexāns eōs, et impōnēns manūs super illōs, benedīcēbat eōs.
phrases.english: And he took them in his arms, laid his hands on them, and blessed them.

phrases.latin: Quod appositum est et appōnētur, Chrīstus benedīcere dignētur.
phrases.english: What is set before us, and what is still to come, may Christ be pleased to bless (a child’s grace).

sources: John C. Traupman, Conversational Latin for Oral Proficiency, p. 280, checked against the searchable text of the book (9 November 2026).
